title: Expanding products of algebraic expressions
summary: Use the distributive law accurately with two or more brackets, then collect like terms and verify the expansion.
objectives: Expand a term across a bracket, including negative terms.
Expand the product of two binomials and collect like terms.
Check an expansion by substitution or reverse factorisation.

sections.title: The distributive law controls every expansion

blocks.text: Expanding removes brackets without changing the value of an expression. The distributive law says that a factor outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. Write each product before simplifying; this makes missed terms visible and keeps negative signs attached to the terms they affect.

A negative multiplier changes the sign of every term in the bracket. For example, -3(x-4) becomes -3x+12, because (-3)(-4)=12. Treat subtraction before a bracket as multiplication by -1 rather than changing only the first term.

sections.title: Multiply every term by every term

blocks.text: For two binomials, each term in the first bracket must multiply each term in the second. A small multiplication grid or four clearly written products is safer than relying on memory. Only after all products are present should like terms be collected.

The leading term comes from multiplying the variable terms; the constant term comes from multiplying the constants. The two middle products often combine. If the brackets contain unlike variables, combine only terms with exactly the same variable part and powers.

sections.title: Collect terms and verify the result

blocks.text: Like terms have identical variable factors and powers. For example, 10x and -3x combine, while 10x and -3x² do not. Arrange a polynomial in descending powers so that omitted or duplicated terms are easier to detect.

A quick check is to substitute a convenient value such as x=1 or x=2 into both the original factored form and the expanded form. Matching values do not prove every step, but a mismatch immediately reveals an error. You can also factor the final expression when the original brackets are obvious.
